title: When a Civil or Commercial Suit Goes to the Delhi High Court Instead of the District Court
meta_description: The pecuniary threshold that sends a Delhi civil suit to the High Court instead of the district court, and how commercial disputes differ.
intro: Where a civil suit gets filed in Delhi turns largely on one number: the value of the claim. Since 2015, the Delhi High Court's original civil jurisdiction has started well above what it used to, and a suit valued below that figure has to go to the district courts whether or not a litigant would prefer the High Court's procedure or its judges. Getting this wrong is not a minor slip; a suit filed at the wrong forum invites an early objection on jurisdiction and, in the worst case, a plaint rejected or returned for refiling at the correct court, with the limitation clock still running in the background.

This guide sets out the current pecuniary threshold for an ordinary civil suit in Delhi, how that threshold interacts with the separate rules for commercial disputes under the Commercial Courts Act, and the practical steps that decide which court actually gets the case.

sections.heading: The current threshold: suits above Rs 2 crore go to the High Court
paragraphs: The Delhi High Court (Amendment) Act, 2015 raised the pecuniary threshold for the High Court's ordinary original civil jurisdiction from Rs 20 lakh to Rs 2 crore, amending Section 5(2) of the Delhi High Court Act, 1966 and the corresponding provision of the Punjab Courts Act, 1918 as applied to Delhi. The amendment came into force on 26 October 2015 by notification of the Ministry of Law and Justice, and from that date a civil suit valued at Rs 2 crore or below has to be filed before the district courts, while one valued above that figure can be filed directly on the original side of the High Court.

A separate notification dated 24 November 2015 transferred suits that were already pending on the High Court's original side, but valued at or below Rs 2 crore, down to the subordinate courts, so the change was applied both prospectively to new filings and retrospectively to the existing backlog rather than only to cases filed after the cut-off date.

sections.heading: How the value of a suit is actually worked out
paragraphs: For a suit for recovery of a specific sum, the value is usually straightforward: it is the amount claimed. Suits for a declaration, an injunction, or specific performance are harder, since there is no single sum being claimed, and valuation there follows the Suits Valuation Act and the Code of Civil Procedure's own rules on how particular kinds of relief are to be valued for the purpose of jurisdiction and court fee. A plaintiff who undervalues a claim to keep it below the Rs 2 crore line, whether to avoid the High Court's fee structure or for any other reason, risks having the valuation challenged by the defendant, and a court can revisit the stated value if the pleadings or the relief actually sought do not support it.

Courts have also had to deal with suits whose value changes after filing, for instance where a plaintiff seeks to amend the plaint to add a claim that pushes the total value past the threshold. Reported Delhi High Court rulings confirm that an amendment application in a suit originally valued below Rs 2 crore can itself raise the jurisdiction question afresh, so an amendment that would increase the value is not something to assume will be allowed without scrutiny of where the suit then properly belongs.

sections.heading: Commercial disputes run on a parallel track
paragraphs: A commercial dispute, broadly covering disputes arising out of ordinary transactions of merchants, bankers, financiers and traders, construction and infrastructure contracts, intellectual property disputes, and several other listed categories under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, is heard by a Commercial Division where the suit is filed in a High Court with ordinary original civil jurisdiction, or by a designated Commercial Court at the district level elsewhere. The Act defines a 'specified value' threshold below which the commercial courts machinery does not apply at all, and a 2018 amendment to the Act reduced that national floor from Rs 1 crore to Rs 3 lakh.

In Delhi specifically, because the High Court's own ordinary original civil jurisdiction only starts above Rs 2 crore, the High Court does not hear commercial suits below that figure even though the Act's national floor is lower. Following the 2018 amendment, the Delhi High Court issued a circular transferring commercial suits valued at or below Rs 2 crore that were pending before it to the district courts, so in practice a commercial dispute valued above Rs 3 lakh but at or below Rs 2 crore is heard by the District Judge sitting as a Commercial Court, and only one valued above Rs 2 crore goes to the Commercial Division of the High Court itself. A constitutional challenge to aspects of the 2018 amendment has been pending before the Delhi High Court, so a litigant with a borderline valuation should check the current position rather than assume this account is final.

sections.heading: Pre-institution mediation is compulsory for most commercial suits
paragraphs: Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act requires a plaintiff to attempt pre-institution mediation before filing a commercial suit, unless the suit contemplates urgent interim relief. The Supreme Court settled a long-running disagreement among High Courts on whether this requirement was mandatory or merely directory in its 2022 decision in Patil Automation Private Limited v. Rakheja Engineers Private Limited, holding that compliance with Section 12A is mandatory and that a plaint filed without attempting it, where no urgent interim relief is genuinely sought, is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The Supreme Court later clarified, in a separate ruling, that this mandatory reading applies prospectively, so a suit filed before 20 August 2022 without pre-institution mediation cannot be rejected on that ground alone under Order VII Rule 11. A plaintiff planning a commercial suit today, however, should treat Section 12A as a genuine precondition and not as a formality that can be cured later by court-referred mediation after the suit is already on file, since the Supreme Court has also held that post-filing mediation does not amount to substantial compliance where no urgent interim relief was actually sought.

sections.heading: What a claimant should check before drafting the plaint
paragraphs: The first practical step is an honest valuation of the relief actually being sought, done before deciding which court to approach, not the other way round. Where the claim is close to the Rs 2 crore line, it is worth setting out in the plaint itself how the valuation was arrived at, since a vague or formulaic valuation clause is one of the first things an opposing counsel will attack at the earliest hearing.

The second is identifying whether the dispute falls within any of the categories the Commercial Courts Act treats as a commercial dispute, since that triggers Section 12A mediation and a different procedural track regardless of which court finally hears it. A dispute between two private individuals over a residential sale agreement, for instance, is unlikely to be commercial in this sense, while a dispute over a construction contract or a supply agreement between businesses usually is, and getting this classification wrong at the outset can mean restarting the pre-suit process after a plaint has already been rejected.

sections.heading: Procedure differs once you are in the right forum
paragraphs: The Delhi High Court's original side runs under its own Original Side Rules, with case management timelines, written statement deadlines and disclosure requirements that are generally stricter than ordinary district court practice, particularly once a suit is also a commercial one and therefore subject to the Commercial Courts Act's own procedural chapter on case management hearings and costs. A litigant used to the pace of an ordinary civil suit at the district court can find the original side's timetable considerably less forgiving of delay, which is worth factoring in when deciding how much time is available to prepare before filing rather than after.

None of this changes the underlying point that forum follows value, not preference. A litigant who would simply rather be heard by the High Court, for reasons of perceived speed or seniority of the bench, cannot get there by inflating the claim beyond what the facts support, and an inflated valuation is as likely to be challenged, and as damaging if it fails, as an undervaluation aimed the other way.

faqs.q: What is the current pecuniary threshold for filing a civil suit directly in the Delhi High Court?
faqs.a: Since the Delhi High Court (Amendment) Act, 2015 took effect on 26 October 2015, a civil suit has to be filed in the Delhi High Court's original side only if it is valued above Rs 2 crore. A suit valued at or below that figure is filed before the district courts.

faqs.q: Can I choose to file in the High Court even if my claim is below Rs 2 crore?
faqs.a: No. The threshold fixes where a suit has to be filed based on its value; it is not a matter of the plaintiff's preference. Filing above the district court's jurisdiction without the claim genuinely supporting that value invites an early challenge on valuation.

faqs.q: Does a commercial dispute below Rs 2 crore ever reach the Delhi High Court?
faqs.a: Generally no, in current Delhi practice. The High Court transferred commercial suits valued at or below Rs 2 crore to the district courts following the 2018 amendment to the Commercial Courts Act, so most such disputes are heard by a District Judge as a Commercial Court instead.

faqs.q: Is pre-suit mediation compulsory before filing a commercial suit in Delhi?
faqs.a: Yes, for suits not seeking urgent interim relief, following the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in Patil Automation. A plaint filed without attempting pre-institution mediation under Section 12A of the Commercial Courts Act can be rejected, though this mandatory reading applies only to suits filed on or after 20 August 2022.

faqs.q: What happens if I deliberately undervalue my suit to avoid the High Court's fees?
faqs.a: The defendant can challenge the stated valuation, and a court can revisit it if the pleadings or relief actually claimed do not support the figure given. An amendment that later raises the claimed value can also reopen the jurisdiction question in a suit originally filed below the threshold.

verification_notes: Rs 2 crore threshold introduced by the Delhi High Court (Amendment) Act, 2015, effective 26 October 2015, amending Section 5(2) of the Delhi High Court Act and the Punjab Courts Act as applied to Delhi: confirmed from two independent sources (ssrana.in and legallyindia.com/scconline) describing the same amendment, section and effective date in consistent terms.

24 November 2015 notification transferring pending original-side suits valued at or below Rs 2 crore to subordinate courts: confirmed from a news report describing this transfer, corroborated by the general description of the same transfer process in a second source discussing the amendment's rollout; treated as confirmed on the transfer mechanism, though the exact notification date rests on the stronger of the two sources.

Suits Valuation Act and CPC rules governing valuation of declaratory and injunction suits, and a Delhi High Court ruling permitting an amendment application to be entertained in a suit originally valued below Rs 2 crore: the general valuation framework is standard civil procedure; the specific ruling is drawn from one law-report headline and is described cautiously as a reported position rather than stated as a general rule.

Commercial Courts Act 2018 amendment reducing the specified value floor from Rs 1 crore to Rs 3 lakh, and the Delhi High Court's circular transferring commercial suits of Rs 2 crore or below to the district courts: confirmed from two independent sources, a PRS India legislative summary of the 2018 amendment and a LiveLaw report on the Delhi High Court's transfer circular.

Pendency of a constitutional challenge to the 2018 amendment before the Delhi High Court: drawn from a single Delhi High Court filing reference found in search results; stated only as a pending challenge with no outcome asserted, since no second source confirming its status was found.

Patil Automation v. Rakheja Engineers (2022) holding Section 12A mandatory, with prospective application from 20 August 2022 and non-substitutability of post-filing mediation: confirmed from Bar and Bench's report of the ruling and corroborated by multiple secondary legal commentary sources describing the same holding and dates in consistent terms.
